newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST-French rate cut seen possible - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-French rate cut seen possible - analysts.

text.p: With the franc holding strong, France has room to cut its key intervention interest rate next Thursday and move toward bringing its rates in line with Germany ahead of European monetary union, economists said on Friday.
"We could see 10 or 15 basis points off the intervention rate next Thursday," said Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney.

He added the spread between the intervention rate -- which sets the floor on money market rates -- and the German repo rate, which it has traditionally tracked, could fall to zero soon after next month's European Union summit in Dublin in mid-December. The meeting is intended to help seal plans for monetary union due to start on January 1, 1999.

"If they (the French) don't (move to parity), it would create a doubt about monetary union," he said. The intervention rate is now at 3.25 percent while the repo rate is at 3.00 percent. Until earlier this year, the Bank of France maintained a spread of at least 35 to 45 basis points over the repo rate.

Other analysts also predicted a cut in the intervention rate on Thursday of 10 to 15 basis. But some believed the central bank would go more slowly to squeeze the maximum impact from easing. They saw a cut of just five basis points on Thursday.
Still, with the franc's robust performance and lower currency risk with the single currency ahead, all agreed parity between the repo and intervention rate was in sight.
The franc was trading at 3.3766 per mark in mid-afternoon, its best level since late April.
Some said it might take several months to achieve rate parity while others saw it happening by the end of January.
"The question is to close the gap with money market rates in Germany. Therefore I believe the Bank of France will lower the intervention rate by 25 basis points in the months ahead," Chaney said.
Already the risk premium on French 10-year government bonds (OATs) over their German counterpart has turned negative.

The intervention rate could go lower than three percent if Germany eases again. Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing seemed to suggest Wednesday the rate-cutting cycle was over in Germany. But on Friday, he and Bundesbank member Ernst Welteke left the door open to more cuts depending on events.

Welteke said a "repo rate cut (in the medium term) is still possible depending on developments" which analysts interpreted as further economic weakness in Germany. "We have to see how the German economy reacts to fiscal tightening," Brossard said.
Analysts noted the franc held up strongly against the mark following Issing's comments Wednesday when other currencies weakened against the German unit.
This, they said, testified to a new-found belief in the franc's strength and belief that monetary union would go ahead.
"In the past, every time the dollar went down the mark gained strength in isolation," Credit Lyonnais bond analyst Iain Lindsay said. "This time, mark-Paris did nothing."
And economists said a record 14 billion franc trade surplus reported for August on Friday was likely to boost the franc further.

"The trade surplus is likely to strengthen the franc further, all the more since some investors begin to seriously consider the possibility of a "final" exchange rate very close to the central rate of one mark to 3.35 francs," Chaney said.
With a single currency in prospect, "there is no reason for the need for the old risk premium (on the intervention rate) to be respected," Lindsay said. Parity "is an achievable target."
